q: What is usually the first sign of puberty in girls?
x: Thelarche, the estrogen-driven breast bud, usually comes first at about age 10; pubic hair follows within months, and menarche arrives 2 to 3 years later.

w.Pubarche: Pubic hair usually follows the breast bud by a few months, driven by adrenal and ovarian androgens.
w.Menarche: The first period is late, arriving 2 to 3 years after the breast bud once estrogen has built the endometrium.
w.Adrenarche: The adrenal androgen rise may start earlier, but it is a hormone event that is not a visible sign of gonadal puberty.
w.Peak height velocity: Girls grow fastest near breast stage 3, about a year before the first period and after the breast bud.

pt.say: In the girls panel, the thelarche bar starts first; pubarche, the growth spurt peak and menarche follow.

q: What testicular volume marks the onset of puberty in boys?
x: A testicular volume of 4 mL or more marks gonadarche in boys, because FSH and LH have begun enlarging the seminiferous tubules.

w.1 mL: One to three milliliters is the normal prepubertal range, so a testis this small shows that puberty has not begun.
w.10 mL: A testis of this size is already well into puberty, around genital stage 3 to 4, not at its first sign.
w.15 mL: Fifteen milliliters is close to adult size, reached in late puberty long after gonadarche begins.
w.25 mL: Twenty-five milliliters is at the upper end of adult testicular size, reached only at the end of puberty.

pt.say: The first bar in the boys panel is testicular enlargement to 4 mL, the size that marks the start of puberty.

q: Which hypothalamic neuropeptide drives GnRH pulses at the onset of puberty?
x: Kisspeptin neurons stimulate GnRH neurons and restart pulsatile GnRH at puberty. Leptin is only permissive, telling the brain that energy stores can support reproduction.

w.Leptin: Leptin comes from fat and is permissive: it signals adequate energy stores and acts partly through kisspeptin neurons, but it is not the direct driver.
w.Dopamine: Dopamine inhibits prolactin release from the pituitary. It is not the driver of GnRH pulses at puberty.
w.Somatostatin: Somatostatin inhibits growth hormone and other pituitary hormones. It does not start GnRH pulses.
w.Ghrelin: Ghrelin is a stomach hormone that signals hunger and tends to suppress, not start, GnRH secretion.

hl: Kisspeptin neurons drive the GnRH pulse generator
pt.say: The top box of the gonadarche engine shows kisspeptin neurons driving the GnRH pulse generator, with leptin permissive; pulsatile GnRH then releases LH and FSH.

q: Which adrenal androgen rises at adrenarche?
x: DHEA-S rises as the zona reticularis matures around ages 6 to 8 under ACTH, independent of GnRH; it causes pubic and axillary hair, body odor and mild acne.

w.Dihydrotestosterone: DHT is made in target tissues from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase; it is not the main adrenal product.
w.Estradiol: Estradiol comes mainly from the ovary during gonadarche and drives breast growth, not the adrenal events of mid-childhood.
w.Cortisol: Cortisol output does not change at adrenarche; the zona reticularis adds androgen without raising glucocorticoid production.
w.Aldosterone: Aldosterone comes from the zona glomerulosa under angiotensin II and has no role in adrenarche.

pt.say: The adrenal engine runs on ACTH, which drives DHEA-S from the maturing zona reticularis; it causes pubic and axillary hair, odor and acne without breast or testis growth.

q: Breast development before what age defines precocious puberty in girls?
x: Pubertal signs before 8 years in girls, or before 9 years in boys, define precocious puberty, so a 7-year-old with breast buds needs evaluation while a 9-year-old usually does not.

w.6 years: Age 6 is younger than the cutoff of 8, so it would miss girls whose breast buds appear between 6 and 8.
w.10 years: Ten is the average age of thelarche, so breast buds at that age are entirely normal.
w.11 years: Breast development at 11 is well within the normal range; it is neither early nor late.
w.13 years: Thirteen is the cutoff for delayed puberty in girls: no breast development by then warrants evaluation.

hl: Signs before age 8 in girls or age 9 in boys
pt.say: The top box states the cutoff: signs before age 8 in girls, or 9 years in boys, define precocious puberty.

q: Which hormone fuses the epiphyseal growth plates in both sexes?
x: Estrogen fuses the growth plates in both sexes; boys make it by aromatizing testosterone, which is why men lacking aromatase or the estrogen receptor stay tall with open epiphyses.

w.Testosterone: Testosterone widens bones and drives growth, but it closes the growth plates only after aromatase converts it to estradiol.
w.Growth hormone: Growth hormone stimulates growth-plate chondrocytes through IGF-1 and lengthens bone; it does not fuse the plates.
w.IGF-1: This factor drives chondrocyte proliferation at the growth plate, lengthening bone rather than closing the plate.
w.DHEA-S: This weak adrenal androgen causes pubic hair and contributes little to skeletal maturation.

pt.say: The Both card states that estrogen fuses the growth plates in both sexes; boys make it by aromatizing testosterone.

q: What is the treatment of central precocious puberty?
x: A continuous GnRH agonist such as depot leuprolide first stimulates, then downregulates pituitary GnRH receptors, so LH, FSH and sex steroids fall, puberty stops and adult height is protected.

w.Pulsatile GnRH: Pulsed GnRH mimics the normal pubertal signal and stimulates LH and FSH; it induces puberty or ovulation rather than stopping it.
w.Aromatase inhibitor: These drugs lower estrogen without stopping the central axis and are used in some peripheral causes, not first-line central disease.
w.Growth hormone: Growth hormone treats growth hormone deficiency and Turner short stature; it does not stop an early pubertal axis.
w.Spironolactone: Spironolactone is an androgen receptor antagonist and cannot suppress the gonadotropins that drive central puberty.

pt.say: The last line of the central column names the treatment: a continuous GnRH agonist, which downregulates the pituitary receptors.

x: A postzygotic activating GNAS mutation keeps the Gs alpha protein on in a mosaic of cells, causing autonomous ovarian estrogen, café-au-lait macules with jagged borders and polyostotic fibrous dysplasia.

w.Inactivating NF1 mutation: Neurofibromatosis type 1 causes smooth-bordered café-au-lait macules and neurofibromas, and its precocious puberty is central, from optic gliomas.
w.Activating LH receptor mutation: This change causes familial testotoxicosis in boys, without skin or bone lesions.
w.Androgen receptor mutation: Androgen receptor mutations cause androgen insensitivity in a 46,XY person, not precocious puberty with skin and bone lesions.
w.Inactivating 21-hydroxylase mutation: Loss of 21-hydroxylase causes an adrenal form of peripheral puberty from androgen excess, not estrogen.

pt.say: The peripheral column lists McCune-Albright (GNAS): an activating GNAS mutation makes ovarian cysts secrete estrogen on their own.

q: Which brain lesion classically causes central precocious puberty in young boys?
x: A hypothalamic hamartoma contains its own GnRH neurons and fires GnRH pulses early, so LH is pubertal. It can cause laughing seizures.

w.Craniopharyngioma: This sellar tumor compresses the pituitary and stalk and usually delays puberty, with growth failure and visual loss.
w.Prolactinoma: Prolactin excess suppresses GnRH and delays puberty or causes amenorrhea; these tumors are rare in young children.
w.Pineal germinoma: These tumors can secrete hCG, which acts at the LH receptor, causing peripheral rather than central puberty in boys.
w.Medulloblastoma: This cerebellar tumor causes ataxia and hydrocephalus and is not a direct source of GnRH pulses.

pt.say: The central column notes that boys often have a lesion, classically a hypothalamic hamartoma that makes its own GnRH pulses.

q: What is the most common cause of delayed puberty?
x: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty is the most common cause, especially in boys: a healthy, short child with a delayed bone age and often a late-maturing parent, whose puberty starts on its own.

w.Kallmann syndrome: Kallmann syndrome causes permanent GnRH deficiency with anosmia and is far less common than a simple lag in the pubertal clock.
w.Turner syndrome: Turner syndrome is the leading cause of ovarian failure in girls with late puberty, but it is rarer than a benign lag overall.
w.Klinefelter syndrome: Klinefelter syndrome is common, yet puberty usually starts on time and then stalls, so it seldom presents as simple lateness.
w.Anorexia nervosa: Anorexia causes functional GnRH suppression in thin girls, an important but less frequent cause than a benign familial lag.

hl: Constitutional delay: the most common cause
pt.say: The first card on the low LH and FSH side is constitutional delay, labeled the most common cause: a healthy, short child with a delayed bone age and often a late-maturing parent.

q: What LH and FSH pattern marks hypergonadotropic hypogonadism?
o: High LH and FSH, low sex steroids
Low LH and FSH, low sex steroids
Low LH and FSH, high sex steroids
High LH and FSH, high sex steroids
Normal LH and FSH, high prolactin
x: High LH and FSH with low sex steroids mean the gonads have failed and the pituitary is pushing against absent feedback, as in Turner syndrome or Klinefelter syndrome; a karyotype comes next.

w.Low LH and FSH, low sex steroids: This is hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, from constitutional delay, Kallmann syndrome or energy deficit, where the signal from above is missing.
w.Low LH and FSH, high sex steroids: Suppressed gonadotropins with raised steroids is the pattern of peripheral precocious puberty, where the steroids come from outside the axis.
w.High LH and FSH, high sex steroids: Raised gonadotropins with raised steroids fits central puberty, or androgen insensitivity, in which the receptor ignores testosterone.
w.Normal LH and FSH, high prolactin: Hyperprolactinemia suppresses GnRH pulses and usually lowers gonadotropins, giving a hypogonadotropic picture.

hl: Primary amenorrhea, FSH and LH high
pt.say: The bottom band names hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, and both panels show why: failed gonads send no feedback, so FSH and LH are high.

q: What does the bone age show in constitutional delay of puberty?
x: Bone age is delayed by about 2 years, matching the child's height age, because the whole pubertal clock runs late and the growth plates stay open longer.

w.Advanced by about 2 years: An advanced skeleton reflects early sex steroid exposure, as in precocious puberty, the opposite of a slow clock.
w.Equal to chronologic age: A skeleton matching the calendar fits a normal child or premature thelarche, not a lag of the whole pubertal clock.
w.Advanced by 4 years: A markedly advanced skeleton signals prolonged sex steroid excess, such as untreated CAH or central precocious puberty.
w.Growth plates already fused: Fused plates mean growth has ended, which happens after puberty and sex steroid exposure, never in a child who has not started.

pt.say: The constitutional delay card lists a bone age delayed about 2 years, so low LH and FSH are normal for that bone age and puberty starts on its own.

q: What distinguishes premature thelarche from central precocious puberty?
o: Normal growth velocity and bone age
x: Premature thelarche is isolated breast budding with normal growth velocity, a bone age near chronologic age and prepubertal LH; central puberty adds a growth spurt, an advancing bone age and pubertal LH.

w.Pubertal basal LH: A pubertal LH shows the GnRH axis has woken, the defining feature of true central puberty rather than a benign variant.
w.Advanced bone age: An advancing skeletal age reflects sustained estrogen exposure and points toward true puberty, not isolated breast budding.
w.Vaginal bleeding: Bleeding means substantial estrogen exposure, from central puberty or an autonomous ovarian cyst, not a benign variant.
w.Rapidly enlarging breasts: Rapid progression suggests true puberty; premature thelarche is stable or regresses over months.

pt.say: The normal-variant column lists no growth acceleration and bone age near normal, the features that separate premature thelarche from central puberty.

q: Which pubertal change in a boy is a normal variant that usually resolves?
x: Tender breast enlargement, pubertal gynecomastia, affects about half of boys in mid-puberty because estradiol briefly rises faster than testosterone; it usually resolves within one to two years.

w.Enlargement of one testis: Unilateral testicular growth suggests a Leydig cell tumor or other mass and needs ultrasound, not reassurance.
w.Galactorrhea: Milk discharge in a boy suggests hyperprolactinemia, such as a prolactinoma, and needs a prolactin level and imaging.
w.Pubic hair at age 6: Sexual hair before age 9 in a boy is precocious and calls for evaluation of adrenal or central causes.
w.Testes under 4 mL at 15: Prepubertal testes past the age-14 cutoff mean delayed puberty and warrant a work-up.

pt.say: The last card of the gonadarche panel describes tender pubertal gynecomastia in mid-puberty as transient: estradiol briefly outruns testosterone, so it needs only reassurance.
